t: Print every element with its index
layman: You are calling out a class attendance register. For each seat you say the seat number and then the student in it.
task: Given an array, print each element together with its index in the format index -> value.
approach: You need the position, not just the value — so use the indexed loop, not for-each.
Start i at 0 because the first box is box 0.
Stop when i reaches length. Not length itself, or you fall off the end.
pseudo:
START
  arr <- [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]
  FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1
      PRINT i, "->", arr[i]
  END FOR
END
trap: Writing i <= arr.length. At i = 7 there is no box, so Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and Python throws IndexError.
cx: Time O(n) — one visit per box · Space O(1)

t: Print the first and the last element
layman: The first person in the queue and the last person in the queue. The last one is not at position 7 — it is at position 6.
task: Print the first element and the last element of an array without using a loop.
approach: First box is always index 0.
Last box is always index length - 1.
No loop needed — jumping to a box by index is instant.
pseudo:
START
  PRINT arr[0]
  PRINT arr[length(arr) - 1]
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

print("First =", arr[0])
print("Last  =", arr[-1])   # -1 means last in Python
trap: Using arr[arr.length] for the last element. Length is a count (7 boxes), index is a position (0 to 6).
cx: Time O(1) — direct jump, no walking · Space O(1)

t: Sum of all elements
layman: Adding up every bill in your wallet. You keep a running total in your head and add each note to it.
task: Find the total of all elements in the array.
approach: Create the total variable OUTSIDE the loop, starting at 0.
Inside the loop, add the current value to the total.
Print after the loop finishes — not inside it.
pseudo:
START
  sum <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      sum <- sum + x
  END FOR
  PRINT sum
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

total = 0
for x in arr:
    total = total + x

print(total)
# shortcut: print(sum(arr))
trap: Declaring int sum = 0; inside the loop. It resets to 0 every round and you end up printing only the last element.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Average of the array
layman: Total marks divided by number of students. The trap: in Java, dividing two whole numbers throws away the decimal.
task: Find the average value of the array, correct to decimals.
approach: Get the sum first (problem 3).
Divide by the number of elements.
In Java, 80 / 7 gives 11 because both are integers. Convert one side to double.
pseudo:
START
  sum <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      sum <- sum + x
  END FOR
  avg <- sum / count(arr)      // as decimal
  PRINT avg
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

total = 0
for x in arr:
    total += x

avg = total / len(arr)   # Python keeps decimals here
print(avg)
trap: Writing double avg = sum / arr.length;. Java divides as integers first, then stores 11.0. Cast BEFORE dividing.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Find the maximum element
layman: A boxing tournament. Start with the weakest possible champion, and let every element fight it. Whoever wins stays champion.
task: Find the largest value in the array without sorting it.
approach: Set max to the smallest possible number so the first real value definitely beats it.
Walk the array. If the current value beats max, it becomes the new max.
Safer alternative: set max = arr[0] and start the loop at 1.
pseudo:
START
  max <- VERY SMALL NUMBER
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x > max THEN
          max <- x
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT max
END
trap: Starting with int max = 0;. If the array is all negative — like [-5, -10, -3] — your answer becomes 0, which is not even in the array.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Find the minimum element
layman: Same tournament, reversed. To find the smallest, start with the strongest possible champion so anything real can beat it.
task: Find the smallest value in the array without sorting it.
approach: Set min to the largest possible number.
If the current value is smaller than min, it becomes the new min.
Remember the pair: looking for MAX start at MIN_VALUE, looking for MIN start at MAX_VALUE.
pseudo:
START
  min <- VERY LARGE NUMBER
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x < min THEN
          min <- x
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT min
END
trap: Copying the max code and forgetting to flip the sign. The comparison must become < AND the starting value must become MAX_VALUE.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Find maximum and minimum in one pass
layman: Walking through the shop once and noting both the costliest and the cheapest item — instead of walking the shop twice.
task: Find both the largest and smallest value using only ONE loop.
approach: Keep two champion variables instead of one.
At every box, run two separate if checks — one for max, one for min.
Two loops would also give the right answer, but that is 2n work instead of n.
pseudo:
START
  max <- arr[0]
  min <- arr[0]
  FOR i FROM 1 TO length(arr) - 1
      IF arr[i] > max THEN max <- arr[i]
      IF arr[i] < min THEN min <- arr[i]
  END FOR
  PRINT max, min
END
trap: Using else if for the min check. If a value updates max, the else blocks the min check — usually still correct here, but it hides the fact that these are two independent questions.
cx: Time O(n) — still one pass · Space O(1)

t: Second largest element without sorting
layman: Gold medal and silver medal. When a new gold winner appears, the old gold becomes silver — that single line is the whole problem.
task: Find the second largest value in the array. Do not sort it.
approach: Keep two variables: first and second.
If x beats first, then second takes the old first, and first becomes x. Order of those two lines matters.
If x only beats second and is not equal to first, update second alone.
pseudo:
START
  first  <- VERY SMALL
  second <- VERY SMALL
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x > first THEN
          second <- first
          first  <- x
      ELSE IF x > second AND x != first THEN
          second <- x
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT second
END
trap: Writing first = x; before second = first;. Then second copies the NEW gold and you print the maximum twice.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — beats sort-and-pick, which is O(n log n)

t: Count elements greater than 10
layman: A teacher marking how many students scored above the cut-off. One tally mark per qualifying student.
task: Count how many elements in the array are greater than 10.
approach: Counter starts at 0 outside the loop.
At each element, ask the condition. If true, add 1 to the counter.
You only need the value here, so for-each is fine.
pseudo:
START
  count <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x > 10 THEN
          count <- count + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
trap: Printing inside the loop. You then see 1 2 3 4 instead of the single final answer 4.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Count even and odd numbers
layman: Splitting a pile of coins into two boxes. The remainder after dividing by 2 decides which box a number goes into.
task: Count how many numbers in the array are even and how many are odd.
approach: x % 2 gives the remainder. 0 means even, anything else means odd.
Keep two counters and use if/else — a number cannot be both.
For negative numbers, checking != 0 is safer than checking == 1.
pseudo:
START
  even <- 0
  odd  <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x MOD 2 = 0 THEN
          even <- even + 1
      ELSE
          odd <- odd + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT even, odd
END
trap: Testing x % 2 == 1 for odd. In Java, -3 % 2 gives -1, so negative odd numbers get counted as even.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Count how many times a value appears
layman: How many times does the number 17 appear in the register? You cannot stop at the first one — you must check every entry.
task: Count the number of occurrences of a given key in the array.
approach: Counter starts at 0.
Compare each element with the key using ==.
Do NOT break — breaking stops at the first match and gives you 1.
pseudo:
START
  count <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x = key THEN
          count <- count + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11, 17, 17]
key = 17

count = 0
for x in arr:
    if x == key:
        count += 1

print(count)
# shortcut: print(arr.count(key))
trap: Adding break; out of habit. Counting needs a full pass; only searching for existence is allowed to stop early.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Sum of elements at even indices
layman: Collect money only from seats 0, 2, 4, 6. The rule is about the seat number, not about the money in it.
task: Find the sum of elements sitting at even index positions.
approach: The condition is on i, not on arr[i] — so for-each cannot work here.
Use the indexed loop and check i % 2 == 0.
Faster version: start i at 0 and jump by 2 with i += 2.
pseudo:
START
  sum <- 0
  FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1 STEP 2
      sum <- sum + arr[i]
  END FOR
  PRINT sum
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

total = 0
for i in range(0, len(arr), 2):
    total += arr[i]

print(total)
trap: Confusing "even index" with "even value". Index 0 holds 14 — that qualifies by index, and it would also qualify by value, which hides the bug until a test case separates them.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Reverse the array in place
layman: Two students stand at the two ends of a row and swap seats, then both step inward. This is your first real two-pointer.
task: Reverse the array using the same array — do not create a second array.
approach: Put left at 0 and right at length - 1.
Swap the two values using a temp variable, then move left forward and right backward.
Stop when they meet or cross — you only need half the passes.
pseudo:
START
  left  <- 0
  right <- length(arr) - 1
  WHILE left < right
      temp       <- arr[left]
      arr[left]  <- arr[right]
      arr[right] <- temp
      left  <- left + 1
      right <- right - 1
  END WHILE
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1

while left < right:
    arr[left], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[left]
    left += 1
    right -= 1

print(arr)
trap: Looping all the way to the end instead of stopping at the middle. Every pair gets swapped twice and the array comes back to its original order.
cx: Time O(n) — n/2 swaps · Space O(1) — no second array

t: Linear search — return the index
layman: Looking for a name in an unsorted attendance sheet. You read from the top until you find it, and you report which line it was on.
task: Find the index of a key in the array. If it is not present, return -1.
approach: You need the position, so use the indexed loop.
The moment you find it, return that index — no reason to keep looking.
If the loop ends without returning, the value is not present. Return -1.
pseudo:
FUNCTION search(arr, key)
  FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1
      IF arr[i] = key THEN
          RETURN i
      END IF
  END FOR
  RETURN -1
END FUNCTION
trap: Putting return -1; inside the loop as an else. It returns -1 on the very first mismatch, before checking the rest.
cx: Best O(1) (first box) · Worst O(n) (last box or absent) · Space O(1)

t: Check whether a value exists
layman: You do not care where the person is sitting, only whether they came today. A yes/no flag is enough.
task: Return true if the key exists in the array, otherwise false.
approach: Start with a flag set to false — assume not present until proved otherwise.
On a match, set the flag to true and break out immediately.
Break matters here: without it you keep scanning after you already know the answer.
pseudo:
START
  found <- FALSE
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x = key THEN
          found <- TRUE
          BREAK
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT found
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]
key = 17

found = False
for x in arr:
    if x == key:
        found = True
        break

print(found)
# shortcut: print(key in arr)
trap: Setting found = false in an else branch. Every non-matching element after the match wipes out your answer.
cx: Worst O(n) · Space O(1) — this is exactly what a HashSet will later make O(1)

t: Find the first negative number
layman: Scanning a bank statement for the first time you went into overdraft. Once you find it, you stop reading.
task: Print the first negative number and its index. If there is none, print a message.
approach: Track whether you found anything with a flag or by returning early.
Condition is x < 0. Note that 0 itself is not negative.
Break immediately — the word "first" is your signal to stop.
pseudo:
START
  found <- FALSE
  FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1
      IF arr[i] < 0 THEN
          PRINT arr[i], i
          found <- TRUE
          BREAK
      END IF
  END FOR
  IF found = FALSE THEN
      PRINT "No negative number"
  END IF
END
trap: Forgetting the break. You then print every negative number, and the question asked only for the first.
cx: Best O(1) · Worst O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Count positive, negative and zero
layman: Sorting a stack of profit-and-loss slips into three trays: profit, loss, and no change. Every slip lands in exactly one tray.
task: Count how many elements are positive, how many are negative, and how many are zero.
approach: Three counters, one loop.
Use if / else if / else so each element is counted exactly once.
Zero is neither positive nor negative — it needs its own branch.
pseudo:
START
  pos <- 0 ; neg <- 0 ; zero <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x > 0 THEN
          pos <- pos + 1
      ELSE IF x < 0 THEN
          neg <- neg + 1
      ELSE
          zero <- zero + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT pos, neg, zero
END
trap: Using x >= 0 for positive. Zero then gets counted as positive and your zero tray stays empty.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Double every element in the array
layman: Every price in the shop is being doubled. You must actually rewrite the price tag — reading it out loud twice does not change the tag.
task: Multiply every element of the array by 2 and store the result back in the same array.
approach: This is an UPDATE, so you must reach the box itself — index loop only.
Write arr[i] = arr[i] * 2 to put the new value back.
for-each gives you a copy of the value; changing x changes nothing in the array.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1
      arr[i] <- arr[i] * 2
  END FOR
  PRINT arr
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

for i in range(len(arr)):
    arr[i] = arr[i] * 2

print(arr)
trap: Writing for (int x : arr) { x = x * 2; }. This compiles and runs, prints nothing wrong, and leaves the array completely unchanged — the most confusing bug for beginners.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — done in place

t: Cap every value at 10
layman: A shop where no item may cost more than 10. Anything priced higher gets re-tagged to exactly 10; cheaper items stay as they are.
task: Replace every element greater than 10 with 10, and report how many were changed.
approach: Update means index loop.
Condition and assignment together: if arr[i] > 10, set it to 10 and increase the counter.
Elements at exactly 10 must NOT count as changed.
pseudo:
START
  changed <- 0
  FOR i FROM 0 TO length(arr) - 1
      IF arr[i] > 10 THEN
          arr[i] <- 10
          changed <- changed + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT arr, changed
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

changed = 0
for i in range(len(arr)):
    if arr[i] > 10:
        arr[i] = 10
        changed += 1

print(arr)
print("Changed =", changed)
trap: Using >= instead of >. A value that is already 10 gets "changed" to 10 and inflates your count.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Count elements divisible by 3
layman: Arranging students into groups of exactly three. A number is divisible by 3 when dividing it leaves nothing left over.
task: Count how many elements in the array are divisible by 3.
approach: Divisible means the remainder is 0.
Use x % 3 == 0 as the condition.
Only the value matters, so for-each is fine.
pseudo:
START
  count <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF x MOD 3 = 0 THEN
          count <- count + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
trap: Writing x / 3 == 0. That asks whether the quotient is zero, which is a completely different question.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Print all pairs in the array
layman: Everyone in the class shakes hands with everyone else. The outer loop picks one person, the inner loop walks through the rest.
task: Print every unique pair of elements (order within a pair does not matter).
approach: Outer loop i picks the first element.
Inner loop j starts at i + 1 so a pair is never repeated and nothing pairs with itself.
Count the printed lines — for n = 4 you get 6, which is n(n-1)/2.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      FOR j FROM i + 1 TO n - 1
          PRINT arr[i], arr[j]
      END FOR
  END FOR
END
trap: Starting j at 0. You then print (14,14), and you print both (14,3) and (3,14) — 16 lines instead of 6.
cx: Time O(n²) — roughly n²/2 pairs · Space O(1)

t: Brute force pair sum — does a pair exist?
layman: Trying every possible pair of notes in your wallet to see if any two add up to the bill amount. Slow, but it definitely works.
task: Given an array and a target, check whether any two different elements add up to the target.
approach: Outer loop fixes one number, inner loop tries every later number with it.
If the two add up to the target, print and stop.
This is the honest first solution — the O(n²) baseline every optimisation is measured against.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      FOR j FROM i + 1 TO n - 1
          IF arr[i] + arr[j] = target THEN
              PRINT arr[i], arr[j]
              RETURN TRUE
          END IF
      END FOR
  END FOR
  RETURN FALSE
END
trap: A single break inside the inner loop only escapes the inner loop. The outer loop continues unless you also stop it — that is why the flag appears in the outer condition.
cx: Worst O(n²) · Space O(1) — two pointers will make this O(n log n), hashing O(n)

t: Count all pairs with a given sum
layman: Now you cannot stop at the first matching pair — the question is how many pairs work, so every combination must be tested.
task: Count how many pairs of elements add up to the given target.
approach: Same nested loop shape as problem 22.
Replace the early return with count++ so the scan continues.
Duplicate values create separate valid pairs — both 5s pair with 15.
pseudo:
START
  count <- 0
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      FOR j FROM i + 1 TO n - 1
          IF arr[i] + arr[j] = target THEN
              count <- count + 1
          END IF
      END FOR
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
trap: Adding break after count++. You would then count at most one pair per outer element and miss the rest.
cx: Time O(n²) · Space O(1)

t: Find duplicates using nested loops
layman: Comparing every answer sheet with every other answer sheet to spot copies. It works, but for 1,000 sheets that is five lakh comparisons.
task: Print every value that appears more than once in the array, using only loops.
approach: Outer loop takes one element, inner loop checks all elements after it.
If two match, that value is a duplicate.
Starting j at i + 1 also prevents printing the same duplicate pair twice.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      FOR j FROM i + 1 TO n - 1
          IF arr[i] = arr[j] THEN
              PRINT arr[i]
              BREAK
          END IF
      END FOR
  END FOR
END
trap: Comparing with i != j instead of starting j at i + 1. Every duplicate then gets printed twice, once from each direction.
cx: Time O(n²) · Space O(1) — a HashSet will bring this down to O(n)

t: Check whether the array is already sorted
layman: Walking down a line of students to check whether each one is taller than the person before. One shorter person and the answer is no.
task: Return true if the array is sorted in ascending order, false otherwise.
approach: Compare neighbours, not the whole array. Check arr[i] against arr[i-1].
Start i at 1 so arr[i-1] always exists.
One violation is enough — set false and break.
pseudo:
START
  sorted <- TRUE
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      IF arr[i] < arr[i - 1] THEN
          sorted <- FALSE
          BREAK
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT sorted
END
trap: Starting the loop at i = 0 and reading arr[i - 1]. At i = 0 that is arr[-1] — an exception in Java, and silently the LAST element in Python, which gives a wrong answer with no error.
cx: Best O(1) · Worst O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Bubble sort — write it yourself
layman: Comparing two neighbours at a time and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. After one full pass, the largest value has bubbled to the end — like the heaviest bubble rising last.
task: Sort the array in ascending order using bubble sort. Do not use any built-in sort.
approach: Inner loop compares arr[j] with arr[j+1] and swaps if the left one is bigger.
After pass 1 the largest is parked at the end, so the inner loop can stop one step earlier each time — that is the "- i".
Outer loop runs n-1 times because the last element needs no pass of its own.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 2
      FOR j FROM 0 TO n - 2 - i
          IF arr[j] > arr[j + 1] THEN
              SWAP arr[j], arr[j + 1]
          END IF
      END FOR
  END FOR
END
trap: Writing j < arr.length in the inner loop. At the last j, arr[j+1] does not exist and you get an out-of-bounds error.
cx: Best O(n) with an early-exit flag · Average and worst O(n²) · Space O(1)

t: Selection sort
layman: Scanning the whole remaining line, picking the shortest person, and making them stand at the front. Then repeat with the rest.
task: Sort the array in ascending order using selection sort.
approach: For each position i, scan the rest of the array to find the index of the minimum.
Swap that minimum into position i.
Unlike bubble sort, there is at most ONE swap per pass — useful when swapping is expensive.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 2
      minIndex <- i
      FOR j FROM i + 1 TO n - 1
          IF arr[j] < arr[minIndex] THEN
              minIndex <- j
          END IF
      END FOR
      SWAP arr[i], arr[minIndex]
  END FOR
END
trap: Tracking the minimum VALUE instead of its INDEX. You cannot swap without knowing where the value lives.
cx: Best, average and worst all O(n²) — it always scans · Space O(1)

t: Insertion sort
layman: Arranging playing cards in your hand. You pick the next card and slide it backwards until it sits in the right place among the already-sorted cards.
task: Sort the array in ascending order using insertion sort.
approach: Treat the left part of the array as already sorted; start from index 1.
Hold the current value in a variable, then shift bigger elements one step right.
Drop the held value into the gap that opens up.
pseudo:
START
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      key <- arr[i]
      j   <- i - 1
      WHILE j >= 0 AND arr[j] > key
          arr[j + 1] <- arr[j]
          j <- j - 1
      END WHILE
      arr[j + 1] <- key
  END FOR
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8]

for i in range(1, len(arr)):
    key = arr[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and arr[j] > key:
        arr[j + 1] = arr[j]
        j -= 1
    arr[j + 1] = key

print(arr)
trap: Forgetting the j >= 0 guard in the while condition. When the key is the smallest, j runs to -1 and you index out of bounds.
cx: Best O(n) when nearly sorted · Worst O(n²) · Space O(1)

t: Sort using the built-in sort
layman: You have now built sorting by hand, so you know what it costs. In real code you usually hand the job to the library, which is far faster than bubble sort.
task: Sort the array in ascending order using the language built-in, and print it before and after.
approach: Arrays.sort in Java needs the import java.util.Arrays line.
It sorts the SAME array — it does not hand you a new one.
Java uses dual-pivot quicksort for int arrays, giving O(n log n).
pseudo:
START
  PRINT arr
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  PRINT arr
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]

print("Before:", arr)

arr.sort()          # changes arr itself
# new_list = sorted(arr)   # keeps the original

print("After: ", arr)
trap: Writing arr = Arrays.sort(arr);. The method returns nothing, so this will not even compile. Just call it on its own line.
cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1) for primitives · Warning: original positions are destroyed

t: Sort in descending order
layman: Largest first, like a rank list. The easiest honest way: sort normally, then read the array backwards.
task: Print the array in descending order using two different methods.
approach: Method 1: sort ascending, then loop from the last index down to 0.
Method 2 in Java: use Integer[] with Collections.reverseOrder() — it needs objects, not primitive int.
Method 2 in Python: sort(reverse=True) — much simpler.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  FOR i FROM n - 1 DOWN TO 0
      PRINT arr[i]
  END FOR
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17]

# Method 1 - read backwards
arr.sort()
for i in range(len(arr) - 1, -1, -1):
    print(arr[i], end=" ")
print()

# Method 2 - one line
arr.sort(reverse=True)
print(arr)
trap: Trying Arrays.sort(intArray, Collections.reverseOrder()) on a primitive int[]. It will not compile — reverseOrder needs Integer objects.
cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1)

t: Kth smallest and Kth largest element
layman: The 3rd rank holder in a class list. Once the list is in order, rank 3 is simply the 3rd row — position k-1 because counting starts at 0.
task: Find the kth smallest and kth largest element in the array.
approach: Sort the array first — that turns ranking into simple indexing.
kth smallest sits at index k - 1.
kth largest sits at index n - k.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  smallest <- arr[k - 1]
  largest  <- arr[n - k]
  PRINT smallest, largest
END
py:
arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]
k = 3

arr.sort()

print(k, "rd largest  =", arr[len(arr) - k])

t: Remove duplicates from a sorted array
layman: In a sorted list, copies sit next to each other. So you only need to compare each item with the one before it — no searching required.
task: Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in place and return the new length.
approach: Keep a writer pointer k that marks where the next unique value should be written.
Reader pointer i walks the array. If arr[i] differs from arr[k], it is new.
Because the array is sorted, one comparison with the previous kept value is enough.
pseudo:
START
  IF n = 0 THEN RETURN 0
  k <- 0
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      IF arr[i] != arr[k] THEN
          k <- k + 1
          arr[k] <- arr[i]
      END IF
  END FOR
  RETURN k + 1
END

arr = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4]

k = 0
for i in range(1, len(arr)):
    if arr[i] != arr[k]:
        k += 1
        arr[k] = arr[i]

print("Length =", k + 1)
print(arr[:k + 1])
trap: Applying this to an UNSORTED array. Duplicates that are far apart never get compared, so they survive.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — no second array

t: Find the median of an array
layman: The middle value once everyone is standing in height order. If two people share the middle, you take the average of both.
task: Find the median. For an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values.
approach: Sort first — median has no meaning in an unsorted array.
Odd length: the single middle element at index n/2.
Even length: average of indices n/2 - 1 and n/2, and the answer may be a decimal.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  IF n is ODD THEN
      median <- arr[n / 2]
  ELSE
      median <- (arr[n/2 - 1] + arr[n/2]) / 2.0
  END IF
  PRINT median
END

arr.sort()

n = len(arr)
if n % 2 == 1:

else:

print(median)
trap: Dividing by 2 instead of 2.0 in Java. (8 + 11) / 2 gives 9 instead of 9.5.
cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1)

t: Count distinct elements after sorting
layman: Once the list is sorted, counting how many different values exist is just counting how many times the value changes as you walk down.
task: Count how many distinct values exist in the array.
approach: Sort so that identical values become neighbours.
Count the first element as 1, then add 1 whenever arr[i] differs from arr[i-1].
A HashSet does this without sorting — you will meet that version in the hashing set.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  count <- 1
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      IF arr[i] != arr[i - 1] THEN
          count <- count + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END

arr.sort()

count = 1
for i in range(1, len(arr)):

print(count)
# shortcut: print(len(set(arr)))

cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1)

t: Check whether two arrays contain the same elements
layman: Two students claim they have the same set of coins in different order. Line both sets up in order and compare them position by position.
task: Check whether two arrays contain exactly the same elements, ignoring order.
approach: First compare lengths — different lengths mean an instant false.
Sort both arrays.
Compare index by index; a single mismatch ends it.
pseudo:
START
  IF length(a) != length(b) THEN RETURN FALSE
  SORT a ; SORT b
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      IF a[i] != b[i] THEN RETURN FALSE
  END FOR
  RETURN TRUE
END
trap: Comparing arrays with a == b in Java. That compares memory addresses, not contents, and is almost always false.
cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1)

t: Palindrome check with two pointers
layman: Two people read the word from opposite ends and walk toward the middle. If they ever read different letters, it is not a palindrome.
task: Check whether a given string reads the same forwards and backwards.
approach: left starts at 0, right starts at length - 1.
If the two characters differ, answer false immediately.
Otherwise move both inward. Stop when they meet — you have checked every pair.
pseudo:
START
  left  <- 0
  right <- length(s) - 1
  WHILE left < right
      IF s[left] != s[right] THEN
          RETURN FALSE
      END IF
      left  <- left + 1
      right <- right - 1
  END WHILE
  RETURN TRUE
END
trap: Comparing strings with == in Java. For characters == is correct, but for String objects you must use .equals().
cx: Time O(n/2) = O(n) · Space O(1) — half the work of building a reversed copy

t: Pair sum with two pointers
layman: Two fingers on a sorted list. Sum too small? Move the left finger right for a bigger number. Sum too big? Move the right finger left for a smaller one.
task: Given an array and a target, find a pair of values that add up to the target. Better than O(n²).
approach: Sort first — the whole method depends on knowing which direction gives bigger values.
left at 0, right at the end. Compute the sum of the two.
Three cases only: equal means found, smaller means left++, larger means right--.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  left  <- 0
  right <- n - 1
  WHILE left < right
      sum <- arr[left] + arr[right]
      IF sum = target THEN
          PRINT arr[left], arr[right] ; BREAK
      ELSE IF sum < target THEN
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE
          right <- right - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
END
trap: Using this on an unsorted array. Without order, moving a pointer does not reliably increase or decrease the sum, and you silently get wrong answers.
cx: Sort O(n log n) + scan O(n) = O(n log n) overall · Space O(1)

t: Count all pairs with a given sum — two pointers
layman: Same two fingers, but now you must keep going after each hit. When you find a match, move BOTH fingers inward and continue counting.
task: Count how many pairs add up to the target, using sorting and two pointers instead of nested loops.
approach: Sort the array first.
On a match, count it and move BOTH pointers — moving only one would recount the same partner.
This version assumes distinct values. When the same value repeats many times, each block of equal values must be counted with multiplication instead.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr ASCENDING
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1 ; count <- 0
  WHILE left < right
      sum <- arr[left] + arr[right]
      IF sum = target THEN
          count <- count + 1
          left  <- left + 1
          right <- right - 1
      ELSE IF sum < target THEN
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE
          right <- right - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
  PRINT count
END

arr = [2, 4, 3, 1, 5]
target = 6
arr.sort()

left, right, count = 0, len(arr) - 1, 0

while left < right:
    total = arr[left] + arr[right]
    if total == target:
        count += 1
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    elif total < target:
        left += 1
    else:
        right -= 1

print(count)
trap: Moving only one pointer after a match. The same element then pairs again with a different partner and inflates the count.
cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1) — versus O(n²) for the nested-loop version

t: Pair with the sum closest to the target
layman: You cannot pay the exact amount, so you look for the pair that is closest to it. You keep a running record of the best near-miss so far.
task: Find the pair whose sum is closest to the given target.
approach: Sort, then use the standard two-pointer walk.
At every step compute the absolute difference from the target and remember the best pair so far.
Move exactly as before: sum too small means left++, too big means right--.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1
  bestDiff <- VERY LARGE
  WHILE left < right
      sum  <- arr[left] + arr[right]
      diff <- ABSOLUTE(target - sum)
      IF diff < bestDiff THEN
          bestDiff <- diff
          bestL <- arr[left] ; bestR <- arr[right]
      END IF
      IF sum < target THEN left <- left + 1
      ELSE right <- right - 1
  END WHILE
  PRINT bestL, bestR
END

arr = [10, 22, 28, 29, 30, 40]
target = 54
arr.sort()

left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
best_diff = float("inf")
best = (0, 0)

while left < right:
    total = arr[left] + arr[right]
    diff = abs(target - total)

    if diff < best_diff:
        best_diff = diff
        best = (arr[left], arr[right])

    if total < target:
        left += 1
    else:
        right -= 1

print(best[0], "and", best[1])
trap: Comparing raw differences without abs(). A sum that overshoots gives a negative difference, which always looks "smaller" and wins wrongly.
cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1)

t: Move all zeros to the end
layman: Empty chairs must all end up at the back. Move every occupied chair forward one by one, then fill whatever is left with empties.
task: Move all zeros to the end while keeping the order of the non-zero elements. Do it in place.
approach: Keep a writer pointer j at the position where the next non-zero should go.
Reader i walks the array. On a non-zero, write it at j and increase j.
After the walk, fill positions j to n-1 with zeros.
pseudo:
START
  j <- 0
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      IF arr[i] != 0 THEN
          arr[j] <- arr[i]
          j <- j + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  WHILE j < n
      arr[j] <- 0
      j <- j + 1
  END WHILE
END
trap: Swapping instead of overwriting, without care. Swapping works too, but overwriting then padding is easier to reason about and keeps the relative order safe.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Move all negative numbers to the left
layman: Two people walk toward each other. The left one stops at a negative in the wrong place, the right one stops at a positive in the wrong place, and they swap.
task: Rearrange the array so that all negative numbers come before all positive numbers.
approach: left starts at 0, right at n-1.
Move left forward while it points at a negative — it is already in place.
Move right backward while it points at a positive. When both are stuck, swap.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1
  WHILE left < right
      IF arr[left] < 0 THEN
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE IF arr[right] >= 0 THEN
          right <- right - 1
      ELSE
          SWAP arr[left], arr[right]
          left <- left + 1 ; right <- right - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
END
trap: Expecting the original relative order to survive. Swapping shuffles the values inside each group — if order matters you need a different approach.
cx: Time O(n) — each pointer moves at most n steps · Space O(1)

t: Merge two sorted arrays
layman: Two sorted queues merging into one. Look at the front person of each queue and let the smaller one enter first.
task: Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array.
approach: Pointer i on the first array, j on the second, k on the result.
Compare a[i] with b[j], copy the smaller one, and advance that pointer only.
When one array runs out, copy whatever is left of the other.
pseudo:
START
  i <- 0 ; j <- 0 ; k <- 0
  WHILE i < len(a) AND j < len(b)
      IF a[i] <= b[j] THEN
          result[k] <- a[i] ; i <- i + 1
      ELSE
          result[k] <- b[j] ; j <- j + 1
      END IF
      k <- k + 1
  END WHILE
  COPY remaining of a INTO result
  COPY remaining of b INTO result
END

b = [2, 4, 6]

i = j = 0

while i < len(a) and j < len(b):

        res.append(a[i]); i += 1
    else:
        res.append(b[j]); j += 1

res.extend(a[i:])
res.extend(b[j:])

print(res)
trap: Skipping the two clean-up loops. Whatever is left in the longer array silently disappears from your result.
cx: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m) for the result

t: Squares of a sorted array, still sorted
layman: Squaring makes negatives positive, so the biggest square comes from either end — never from the middle. Fill the answer from the back.
task: Given a sorted array that may contain negatives, return the squares in sorted order without sorting again.
approach: The largest square is at one of the two ends, because the array is sorted.
Compare the squares at left and right, take the bigger, and place it at the END of the result.
Fill the result backwards using a pointer starting at n - 1.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1 ; pos <- n - 1
  WHILE left <= right
      IF ABS(arr[left]) > ABS(arr[right]) THEN
          result[pos] <- arr[left] * arr[left]
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE
          result[pos] <- arr[right] * arr[right]
          right <- right - 1
      END IF
      pos <- pos - 1
  END WHILE
END

arr = [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]
n = len(arr)
res = [0] * n

left, right, pos = 0, n - 1, n - 1

while left <= right:
    if abs(arr[left]) > abs(arr[right]):
        res[pos] = arr[left] ** 2
        left += 1
    else:
        res[pos] = arr[right] ** 2
        right -= 1
    pos -= 1

print(res)
trap: Using left < right instead of <=. The final middle element never gets squared and stays as 0 in the result.
cx: Time O(n) — beats squaring then sorting, which is O(n log n) · Space O(n)

t: Triplet sum — find three numbers adding to a target
layman: Fix one number, then the problem shrinks to the pair-sum problem you already solved. One loop on the outside, two pointers on the inside.
task: Find whether any three elements add up to the given target.
approach: Sort the array first.
Fix arr[i] with an outer loop, then look for a PAIR summing to target - arr[i].
Run two pointers between i+1 and n-1 — exactly the technique from problem 37.
pseudo:
START
  SORT arr
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 3
      left <- i + 1 ; right <- n - 1
      need <- target - arr[i]
      WHILE left < right
          sum <- arr[left] + arr[right]
          IF sum = need THEN
              PRINT arr[i], arr[left], arr[right] ; RETURN
          ELSE IF sum < need THEN left <- left + 1
          ELSE right <- right - 1
      END WHILE
  END FOR
END
trap: Letting the outer loop run to n - 1. There must be at least two elements after i, so it stops at n - 3.
cx: Time O(n²) — one loop times one pointer scan · Space O(1). Brute force with three loops would be O(n³)

t: Container with the most water
layman: Two walls holding water between them. The water level is set by the shorter wall, so moving the taller wall inward can never help — always move the shorter one.
task: Given heights of vertical lines, find the maximum area of water that can be held between two of them.
io: Input: [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7] Output: 49 (between height 8 at index 1 and height 7 at index 8)
approach: Area = width × height, where width is right - left and height is the smaller of the two walls.
Start with the widest possible pair: left at 0, right at the end.
Move the SHORTER wall inward. Moving the taller one loses width without ever gaining height.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1 ; best <- 0
  WHILE left < right
      height <- MIN(arr[left], arr[right])
      area   <- height * (right - left)
      best   <- MAX(best, area)
      IF arr[left] < arr[right] THEN
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE
          right <- right - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
  PRINT best
END

h = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]

left, right, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0

while left < right:
    height = min(h[left], h[right])
    area = height * (right - left)
    best = max(best, area)

    if h[left] < h[right]:
        left += 1
    else:
        right -= 1

print(best)
trap: Moving the taller wall. Width always shrinks by 1, and the height is still capped by the short wall — so you can only lose area.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — brute force over all pairs would be O(n²)

t: Check whether one string is a subsequence of another
layman: Ticking off letters of a short word as you read a long word left to right. The letters must appear in order, but not necessarily together.
task: Check whether string a appears as a subsequence inside string b.
io: Input: a = "abc", b = "ahbgdc" -> true Input: a = "axc", b = "ahbgdc" -> false
approach: Pointer i on the short string, j on the long string.
Always move j forward. Move i only when the characters match.
If i reaches the end of the short string, every letter was found in order.
pseudo:
START
  i <- 0 ; j <- 0
  WHILE i < len(a) AND j < len(b)
      IF a[i] = b[j] THEN
          i <- i + 1
      END IF
      j <- j + 1
  END WHILE
  RETURN i = len(a)
END
trap: Moving j only on a match. Then a single mismatch freezes both pointers and the loop never ends.
cx: Time O(n) where n is the longer string · Space O(1)

t: Reverse only the vowels in a string
layman: Two people walk in from both ends but only stop at vowels. They ignore every consonant, and swap when both have stopped.
task: Reverse only the vowels of a string, leaving all other characters in place.
approach: left and right pointers as usual.
Skip left forward while it is not a vowel; skip right backward while it is not a vowel.
When both are on vowels, swap and move both inward.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1
  WHILE left < right
      IF s[left] is NOT vowel THEN
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE IF s[right] is NOT vowel THEN
          right <- right - 1
      ELSE
          SWAP s[left], s[right]
          left <- left + 1 ; right <- right - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
END
trap: Trying to swap characters inside a Java String directly. Strings are immutable — convert to a char array first.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the character array

t: Two sum on a sorted array — return original indices
layman: Sorting scrambles the seat numbers. If the question asks where the numbers were, you must carry each value along with its original index.
task: Find two values adding to the target and report their ORIGINAL indices, even though you sort to solve it.
io: Input: [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11], target = 25 Output: indices [3, 4] (8 at index 3, 17 at index 4)
approach: Build pairs of (value, original index) before sorting.
Sort those pairs by value, then run the standard two-pointer walk.
When a pair matches, report the stored original indices, not the pointer positions.
pseudo:
START
  BUILD pairs OF (value, originalIndex)
  SORT pairs BY value
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1
  WHILE left < right
      sum <- pairs[left].value + pairs[right].value
      IF sum = target THEN
          PRINT pairs[left].index, pairs[right].index ; BREAK
      ELSE IF sum < target THEN left <- left + 1
      ELSE right <- right - 1
  END WHILE
END

arr = [14, 3, 21, 8, 17, 6, 11]
target = 25

pairs = [(arr[i], i) for i in range(len(arr))]
pairs.sort()

left, right = 0, len(pairs) - 1

while left < right:
    total = pairs[left][0] + pairs[right][0]
    if total == target:
        print([pairs[left][1], pairs[right][1]])
        break
    elif total < target:
        left += 1
    else:

cx: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n) for the pairs. The HashMap version solves this in O(n) without sorting

t: Sort an array of 0s and 1s
layman: Separating a mixed pile of black and white beads with two hands: zeros go left, ones go right, in a single pass.
task: Sort an array containing only 0s and 1s without using any sorting function.
approach: left starts at 0, right at n-1.
If arr[left] is 0 it is already home — move left forward.
If arr[right] is 1 it is already home — move right backward. Otherwise swap.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; right <- n - 1
  WHILE left < right
      IF arr[left] = 0 THEN
          left <- left + 1
      ELSE IF arr[right] = 1 THEN
          right <- right - 1
      ELSE
          SWAP arr[left], arr[right]
          left <- left + 1 ; right <- right - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
END
trap: Counting the zeros and rewriting the array is also valid and simpler — but it needs two passes. The two-pointer version does it in one.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s (Dutch flag)
layman: Three buckets and three pointers. Low marks where the next 0 goes, high marks where the next 2 goes, and mid does the walking.
task: Sort an array containing only 0s, 1s and 2s in a single pass, without any sorting function.
approach: low = 0, mid = 0, high = n - 1. Everything before low is 0, everything after high is 2.
If arr[mid] is 0: swap with low, then advance both low and mid.
If arr[mid] is 1: just advance mid. If it is 2: swap with high and decrease high — but do NOT advance mid, because the swapped-in value is unchecked.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; mid <- 0 ; high <- n - 1
  WHILE mid <= high
      IF arr[mid] = 0 THEN
          SWAP arr[low], arr[mid]
          low <- low + 1 ; mid <- mid + 1
      ELSE IF arr[mid] = 1 THEN
          mid <- mid + 1
      ELSE
          SWAP arr[mid], arr[high]
          high <- high - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
END

low = mid = 0
high = len(arr) - 1

while mid <= high:
    if arr[mid] == 0:
        arr[low], arr[mid] = arr[mid], arr[low]
        low += 1
        mid += 1
    elif arr[mid] == 1:
        mid += 1
    else:
        arr[mid], arr[high] = arr[high], arr[mid]
        high -= 1

print(arr)
trap: Advancing mid after swapping with high. The value you just pulled in from the right has never been examined — you must inspect it before moving on.
cx: Time O(n) single pass · Space O(1)

t: HashSet basics — store and check instantly
layman: A guest list at the gate. You cannot ask who is 5th on the list, but you can ask "is this person on the list?" and get an answer instantly.
task: Add values to a set and check whether given values exist. Show that duplicates are ignored.
approach: A set stores UNIQUE values only. Adding a duplicate changes nothing.
contains() answers in constant time on average — it does not scan.
This is the tool that turns "search the whole array" into "just ask".
pseudo:
START
  set <- EMPTY SET
  ADD 10, 20, 30, 10 TO set
  PRINT size(set)
  PRINT set CONTAINS 20
  PRINT set CONTAINS 50
END

s.add(10)
s.add(20)
s.add(30)
s.add(10)      # ignored

trap: Expecting a set to keep insertion order or allow indexing. There is no set[0] — a set only answers membership questions.

t: Find duplicates using a HashSet
layman: At the gate you keep a list of everyone who has already entered. When someone arrives, you ask "have I seen you before?" — one question, no scanning.
task: Print every value that appears more than once, using a HashSet instead of nested loops.
approach: Keep a set of values already seen.
For each element ask: is it already in the set? If yes, it is a duplicate.
If no, add it and continue. One pass, no inner loop.

START
  seen <- EMPTY SET
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF seen CONTAINS x THEN
          PRINT x
      ELSE
          ADD x TO seen
      END IF
  END FOR
END
trap: Adding x to the set before checking. Then every element looks like a duplicate of itself.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n) — compare with problem 24, which was O(n²) and O(1). This is the memory-for-speed trade

t: Count distinct elements with a HashSet
layman: How many different people came to the event? Put every name on the guest list — duplicates collapse automatically — then count the list.
task: Count how many distinct values are in the array, without sorting.
approach: Add every element to a set.
The set silently drops repeats.
The answer is simply the size of the set.
pseudo:
START
  seen <- EMPTY SET
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      ADD x TO seen
  END FOR
  PRINT size(seen)
END

seen = set()
for x in arr:

print(len(seen))
# shortcut: print(len(set(arr)))

t: First repeating element
layman: The first person who comes back for a second helping. Careful: the answer is the one whose repeat happens earliest, not the earliest value.
task: Find the first element that repeats — the one whose second occurrence comes earliest.
approach: Walk left to right with a seen set.
The very first element you find already in the set is the answer.
Stop right there — later repeats are irrelevant.
pseudo:
START
  seen <- EMPTY SET
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF seen CONTAINS x THEN
          PRINT x ; RETURN
      END IF
      ADD x TO seen
  END FOR
  PRINT "No repeating element"
END

for x in arr:
