cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n)

t: Frequency of every element (HashMap)
layman: A tally register with two columns: the value on the left, how many times it appeared on the right. Every time you see it again, you update the right column.
task: Count how many times each value appears in the array and print value -> count.
approach: Key = the value, Value = how many times it has appeared.
If the key already exists, put the old count + 1. If not, put 1.
getOrDefault(x, 0) in Java handles both cases in one line.
pseudo:
START
  freq <- EMPTY MAP
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF freq HAS KEY x THEN
          freq[x] <- freq[x] + 1
      ELSE
          freq[x] <- 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT freq
END
trap: Calling freq.get(x) + 1 without a default. The first time a key appears, get() returns null and Java throws a NullPointerException.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n)

t: First non-repeating element
layman: The first person who came to the party alone. You need two passes: first count everyone, then walk the guest list in order and find the first with a count of 1.
task: Find the first element that appears exactly once in the array.
approach: Pass 1: build the frequency map.
Pass 2: walk the ARRAY again in original order, not the map — map order is not guaranteed.
Return the first value whose count is 1.
pseudo:
START
  freq <- frequency map of arr
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF freq[x] = 1 THEN
          PRINT x ; RETURN
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT "All elements repeat"
END
trap: Looping over the map in pass 2. HashMap has no guaranteed order, so you might return 7 instead of 6. The original array is your source of order.
cx: Time O(n) — two passes is still linear · Space O(n)

t: Most frequent element
layman: Which item did the canteen sell the most? Build the tally register, then find the row with the biggest number in the right column.
task: Find the element that appears the maximum number of times.
approach: Build the frequency map first.
Then run the champion pattern over the map entries: track the best count and the key that owns it.
If two values tie, this version keeps whichever it meets first.
pseudo:
START
  freq <- frequency map of arr
  best <- -1 ; bestCount <- 0
  FOR EACH (key, count) IN freq
      IF count > bestCount THEN
          bestCount <- count
          best <- key
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT best, bestCount
END
trap: Tracking only the maximum count and forgetting to save the key. You end up knowing "3 times" but not which value.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n)

t: Two Sum — the optimised HashMap solution
layman: Instead of asking "which number should I try next?", you ask "have I already walked past the number I need?". That flip is the whole optimisation.
task: Return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target, in one pass, without sorting.
approach: At each element, compute required = target - current.
Ask the map whether required has already been seen. If yes, you have your pair.
If not, store current -> its index and move on. Store AFTER checking, never before.
pseudo:
FUNCTION twoSum(arr, target)
  map <- EMPTY MAP
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      required <- target - arr[i]
      IF map HAS KEY required THEN
          RETURN [ map[required], i ]
      END IF
      map[arr[i]] <- i
  END FOR
  RETURN [-1, -1]
END FUNCTION
trap: Putting the current number into the map before checking. With target 20 and a single 10 in the array, the number would then find itself and report a false pair.
cx: Time O(n) single pass · Space O(n). Compare: brute force O(n²), sorted two-pointer O(n log n) — and this one keeps the original indices

t: Check whether two arrays are anagrams
layman: Two shopping bags with the same items in different order. Count what is in the first bag, then remove one of each as you go through the second. Nothing should be left over.
task: Check whether two arrays contain the same elements with the same counts, in any order.
approach: Different lengths means false immediately.
Build a frequency map from the first array.
Walk the second array, decreasing counts. If a key is missing or its count hits below zero, return false.
pseudo:
START
  IF len(a) != len(b) THEN RETURN FALSE
  freq <- frequency map of a
  FOR EACH x IN b
      IF freq DOES NOT HAVE x OR freq[x] = 0 THEN
          RETURN FALSE
      END IF
      freq[x] <- freq[x] - 1
  END FOR
  RETURN TRUE
END
trap: Only checking that every element of b exists in a. Without counts, [1,1,2] and [1,2,2] would wrongly pass.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n) — the sorting version in problem 35 was O(n log n)

t: Union and intersection of two arrays
layman: Union is everyone who came to either party. Intersection is only those who came to both.
task: Find the union and the intersection of two arrays.
approach: Union: dump both arrays into one set — duplicates vanish by themselves.
Intersection: put the first array in a set, then walk the second and keep whatever the set already contains.
Use a second set for results so repeated matches are not printed twice.
pseudo:
START
  union <- EMPTY SET
  ADD ALL OF a TO union
  ADD ALL OF b TO union

  setA <- SET OF a
  inter <- EMPTY SET
  FOR EACH x IN b
      IF setA CONTAINS x THEN
          ADD x TO inter
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT union, inter
END
py:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
b = [3, 4, 5]

union = set(a) | set(b)
intersection = set(a) & set(b)

print("Union:", union)
print("Intersection:", intersection)
trap: Using nested loops for the intersection. It works, but it costs O(n×m) — the set turns each check into O(1).
cx: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)

t: Find the missing number from 1 to n
layman: A class of 7 roll numbers but only 6 students present. Two ways: tick off names on a list, or use the arithmetic shortcut of expected total minus actual total.
task: An array contains numbers from 1 to n with exactly one missing. Find it.
approach: Set method: put everything in a set, then loop 1..n and report the first number not present.
Math method: the total of 1..n is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum — the difference IS the missing number.
The math method uses no extra memory at all.
pseudo:
// Method 1 - set
  seen <- SET OF arr
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n
      IF seen DOES NOT CONTAIN i THEN PRINT i
  END FOR

// Method 2 - maths
  expected <- n * (n + 1) / 2
  actual   <- SUM of arr
  PRINT expected - actual
py:
arr = [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]
n = 7

# Method 1 - set
seen = set(arr)
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    if i not in seen:
        print("Missing (set):", i)

# Method 2 - maths
expected = n * (n + 1) // 2
print("Missing (maths):", expected - sum(arr))
trap: Writing n * (n + 1) / 2 with a very large n in Java. The multiplication can overflow int before the division — use long for big inputs.
cx: Set method: O(n) time, O(n) space · Maths method: O(n) time, O(1) space

t: Count pairs with a given difference
layman: Instead of testing every pair, ask at each number: "is the partner I need already on my list?" — exactly the Two Sum flip, but with subtraction.
task: Count how many pairs of elements have a difference equal to k.
approach: Put every element in a set first.
For each x, check whether x + k exists in the set.
Each qualifying x contributes one pair — no nested loop needed.
pseudo:
START
  seen <- SET OF arr
  count <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF seen CONTAINS (x + k) THEN
          count <- count + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
py:
arr = [1, 5, 3, 4, 2]
k = 2

seen = set(arr)

count = 0
for x in arr:
    if x + k in seen:
        count += 1

print(count)
trap: Checking both x + k and x - k. Every pair then gets counted twice — check one direction only.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n) — nested loops would be O(n²)

t: Duplicate within k positions
layman: A sliding guest list that only remembers the last k people. If someone shows up again while still on that short list, you have your answer.
task: Check whether the array contains a duplicate pair that are at most k indices apart.
approach: Keep a set holding only the last k elements you passed.
If the current element is already in that window set, the duplicate is close enough — return true.
Once the set grows past k, remove the element that fell out of range.
pseudo:
START
  window <- EMPTY SET
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      IF window CONTAINS arr[i] THEN RETURN TRUE
      ADD arr[i] TO window
      IF size(window) > k THEN
          REMOVE arr[i - k] FROM window
      END IF
  END FOR
  RETURN FALSE
END
trap: Never removing old elements. The set then remembers everything and reports duplicates that are far apart.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(k) — only the window is stored

t: Longest run of consecutive numbers
layman: Roll numbers scattered on the floor. You only start counting a chain from a number whose predecessor is missing — that is where a chain truly begins.
task: Find the length of the longest sequence of consecutive numbers in the array. Order in the array does not matter.
approach: Put everything in a set for instant lookups.
For each x, first check whether x - 1 exists. If it does, x is in the middle of a chain — skip it.
If x - 1 is absent, x starts a chain. Count forward with x+1, x+2, … while they exist.
pseudo:
START
  seen <- SET OF arr
  best <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN seen
      IF seen DOES NOT CONTAIN (x - 1) THEN
          length <- 1
          next <- x + 1
          WHILE seen CONTAINS next
              length <- length + 1
              next <- next + 1
          END WHILE
          best <- MAX(best, length)
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
py:
arr = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]
seen = set(arr)

best = 0

for x in seen:
    if x - 1 not in seen:
        length = 1
        nxt = x + 1
        while nxt in seen:
            length += 1
            nxt += 1
        best = max(best, length)

print(best)
trap: Counting a chain from every element. Then 1,2,3,4 gets walked four times and the solution degrades to O(n²). The "is x-1 absent?" guard is what keeps it linear.
cx: Time O(n) — each number is visited at most twice · Space O(n). Sorting would give O(n log n)

t: Check whether an array contains any duplicate
layman: Just a yes-or-no question: did anyone enter twice? The moment you catch one repeat, you can stop checking.
task: Return true if any value appears at least twice, otherwise false.
approach: Add each element to a set as you walk.
If add() returns false in Java, that value was already there — an instant duplicate signal.
Shortcut: if the set size ends up smaller than the array length, duplicates existed.
pseudo:
START
  seen <- EMPTY SET
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      IF seen CONTAINS x THEN RETURN TRUE
      ADD x TO seen
  END FOR
  RETURN FALSE
END
trap: Building the whole set first and only then comparing sizes. Correct, but it always does the full pass — the early return can stop at element 2.
cx: Best O(1) · Worst O(n) · Space O(n)

t: Build a prefix sum array
layman: A bank passbook. Each row shows not just today deposit but the balance so far. Once you have balances, any period total is one subtraction away.
task: Build an array where each position holds the sum of all elements up to that position.
approach: The first prefix value is just the first element.
From then on: prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + arr[i]. You reuse the previous answer instead of re-adding.
This costs one pass, and it is what makes range queries instant afterwards.
pseudo:
START
  prefix[0] <- arr[0]
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      prefix[i] <- prefix[i - 1] + arr[i]
  END FOR
  PRINT prefix
END
py:
arr = [2, 3, 5, 4]
prefix = [0] * len(arr)

prefix[0] = arr[0]

for i in range(1, len(arr)):
    prefix[i] = prefix[i - 1] + arr[i]

print(prefix)
trap: Starting the loop at i = 0 with prefix[i-1]. Index -1 crashes in Java and silently reads the last element in Python.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n)

t: Range sum queries using prefix sum
layman: "How much did I spend from March to July?" = balance at July minus balance at February. One subtraction, no matter how many months.
task: Answer many queries of the form "sum of elements from index L to R" quickly.
approach: Build the prefix array once, in O(n).
For a query: answer = prefix[R] - prefix[L-1].
If L is 0 there is nothing to subtract — answer is just prefix[R]. Handle that case.
pseudo:
START
  BUILD prefix FROM arr
  FUNCTION rangeSum(L, R)
      IF L = 0 THEN
          RETURN prefix[R]
      ELSE
          RETURN prefix[R] - prefix[L - 1]
      END IF
  END FUNCTION
END
py:
arr = [2, 3, 5, 4, 1, 6]

prefix = [0] * len(arr)
prefix[0] = arr[0]
for i in range(1, len(arr)):
    prefix[i] = prefix[i - 1] + arr[i]

def range_sum(L, R):
    if L == 0:
        return prefix[R]
    return prefix[R] - prefix[L - 1]

print(range_sum(1, 3))
print(range_sum(0, 2))
trap: Using prefix[R] - prefix[L]. That drops arr[L] from the total. You must subtract everything BEFORE L, which is prefix[L-1].
cx: Build O(n) once · Each query O(1) · Space O(n). Recomputing every query would be O(n) per query

t: Equilibrium index
layman: A see-saw balance point: a position where the weight on the left equals the weight on the right, ignoring the person standing on the pivot.
task: Find an index where the sum of all elements to its left equals the sum of all elements to its right.
io: Input: [1, 3, 5, 2, 2] Output: 2 (1 + 3 = 4 on the left, 2 + 2 = 4 on the right)
approach: Compute the total sum of the array first.
Walk with a running leftSum. At index i, rightSum = total - leftSum - arr[i].
If they match, i is your answer. Then add arr[i] into leftSum before moving on.
pseudo:
START
  total <- SUM of arr
  leftSum <- 0
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      rightSum <- total - leftSum - arr[i]
      IF leftSum = rightSum THEN
          PRINT i ; RETURN
      END IF
      leftSum <- leftSum + arr[i]
  END FOR
  PRINT -1
END
py:
arr = [1, 3, 5, 2, 2]

total = sum(arr)
left_sum = 0
answer = -1

for i in range(len(arr)):
    right_sum = total - left_sum - arr[i]
    if left_sum == right_sum:
        answer = i
        break
    left_sum += arr[i]

print(answer)
trap: Including arr[i] in one of the two sides. The pivot element belongs to neither — that is why it is subtracted separately.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — no prefix array is even needed

t: Count subarrays with sum equal to k
layman: If the running total was x earlier and it is x + k now, then everything in between adds up to exactly k. So you store every running total you have seen.
task: Count how many continuous subarrays have a sum exactly equal to k.
approach: Keep a running sum as you walk, and a map of running sum -> how many times it has occurred.
At each step ask: have I seen (runningSum - k) before? Each such occurrence is one valid subarray ending here.
Seed the map with sum 0 occurring once, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.
pseudo:
START
  map <- { 0 : 1 }
  sum <- 0 ; count <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      sum <- sum + x
      IF map HAS KEY (sum - k) THEN
          count <- count + map[sum - k]
      END IF
      map[sum] <- map[sum] + 1
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
py:
arr = [1, 2, 3, -3, 1, 1, 1, 4, 2, -3]
k = 3

seen = {0: 1}
total = 0
count = 0

for x in arr:
    total += x
    if total - k in seen:
        count += seen[total - k]
    seen[total] = seen.get(total, 0) + 1

print(count)
trap: Forgetting to seed the map with {0 : 1}. Every subarray that starts at index 0 then goes uncounted.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n) — checking all subarrays by hand would be O(n²)

t: Longest subarray with sum k
layman: Same passbook trick, but now you want the longest stretch. So you store the FIRST time each running total appeared — earliest start gives the longest stretch.
task: Find the length of the longest continuous subarray whose sum equals k.
approach: Keep a running sum and a map of running sum -> the earliest index where it occurred.
If runningSum - k has been seen at index j, the subarray from j+1 to i sums to k. Its length is i - j.
Only store a running sum the FIRST time you see it — storing again would shorten the answer.
pseudo:
START
  map <- EMPTY MAP
  sum <- 0 ; best <- 0
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      sum <- sum + arr[i]
      IF sum = k THEN
          best <- i + 1
      END IF
      IF map HAS KEY (sum - k) THEN
          best <- MAX(best, i - map[sum - k])
      END IF
      IF map DOES NOT HAVE KEY sum THEN
          map[sum] <- i
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
trap: Overwriting the map entry every time a running sum repeats. You must keep the EARLIEST index — a later one gives a shorter subarray.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n)

t: Does a subarray with sum zero exist?
layman: If your bank balance ever returns to a figure it already was, then everything that happened in between cancelled out to zero.
task: Check whether the array has any continuous subarray whose sum is 0.
approach: Track the running sum and store every value it takes in a set.
If the running sum is ever 0, or repeats a value already in the set, a zero-sum subarray exists.
A repeated running sum means the stretch between the two points added up to nothing.
pseudo:
START
  seen <- EMPTY SET
  sum <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      sum <- sum + x
      IF sum = 0 OR seen CONTAINS sum THEN
          RETURN TRUE
      END IF
      ADD sum TO seen
  END FOR
  RETURN FALSE
END
py:
def has_zero_sum(arr):
    seen = set()
    total = 0
    for x in arr:
        total += x
        if total == 0 or total in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(total)
    return False

print(has_zero_sum([4, 2, -3, 1, 6]))
print(has_zero_sum([1, 2, 3]))
trap: Forgetting the sum == 0 check. A subarray starting at index 0 that sums to zero would then be missed.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(n)

t: Product of array except self
layman: For every seat, multiply everything to its left by everything to its right. Two running passes — and division is not allowed, because a single zero would break it.
task: For each index, produce the product of all other elements. Do not use division.
approach: Pass 1 (left to right): store the running product of everything before each index.
Pass 2 (right to left): multiply each stored value by the running product of everything after it.
The same prefix idea, applied in both directions with multiplication.
pseudo:
START
  result[0] <- 1
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      result[i] <- result[i - 1] * arr[i - 1]
  END FOR

  right <- 1
  FOR i FROM n - 1 DOWN TO 0
      result[i] <- result[i] * right
      right <- right * arr[i]
  END FOR
END
py:
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4]
n = len(arr)
res = [1] * n

for i in range(1, n):
    res[i] = res[i - 1] * arr[i - 1]

right = 1
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    res[i] = res[i] * right
    right = right * arr[i]

print(res)
trap: Solving it by computing the total product and dividing. One zero in the array makes every answer wrong, and two zeros crash it.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) extra, if the output array is not counted

t: Split the array into two equal-sum halves
layman: Cutting a chain of weights at one point so both halves weigh the same. Once you know the total, one running sum tells you whether a cut works.
task: Check whether there is a point where the array can be cut into two parts with equal sums.
approach: Find the total. If the total is odd, no equal split can exist — answer false immediately.
Walk with a running left sum. A cut works when leftSum equals total / 2.
No second array is needed — one running number does the job.
pseudo:
START
  total <- SUM of arr
  IF total is ODD THEN RETURN FALSE
  half <- total / 2
  leftSum <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      leftSum <- leftSum + x
      IF leftSum = half THEN RETURN TRUE
  END FOR
  RETURN FALSE
END
trap: Skipping the odd-total check. With an odd total, integer division silently rounds half down and you can get a false positive.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Count subarrays with an even sum
layman: Even minus even is even. Odd minus odd is also even. So you only need to count how many running totals were even and how many were odd.
task: Count how many continuous subarrays have an even sum.
approach: Track the running sum and whether it is even or odd.
Every pair of running totals with the SAME parity forms an even-sum subarray between them.
Keep two counters — evenCount starts at 1 for the empty prefix — and add the matching counter each step.
pseudo:
START
  evenCount <- 1 ; oddCount <- 0
  sum <- 0 ; answer <- 0
  FOR EACH x IN arr
      sum <- sum + x
      IF sum is EVEN THEN
          answer <- answer + evenCount
          evenCount <- evenCount + 1
      ELSE
          answer <- answer + oddCount
          oddCount <- oddCount + 1
      END IF
  END FOR
  PRINT answer
END
py:
arr = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]

even_count, odd_count = 1, 0
total, answer = 0, 0

for x in arr:
    total += x
    if total % 2 == 0:
        answer += even_count
        even_count += 1
    else:
        answer += odd_count
        odd_count += 1

print(answer)
trap: Starting evenCount at 0. The empty prefix has a sum of 0, which is even, and subarrays starting at index 0 depend on it being counted.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — checking every subarray would be O(n²)

t: Maximum subarray sum (Kadane)
layman: Walking a road collecting profit and loss. If your running total goes negative, drop it and start fresh — carrying a loss forward can never help you.
task: Find the largest sum obtainable from any continuous subarray.
approach: Keep current, the best sum ending at this position.
At each element choose: extend the previous run, or start again from this element alone.
Keep best as the champion of all current values seen so far.
pseudo:
START
  current <- arr[0]
  best    <- arr[0]
  FOR i FROM 1 TO n - 1
      current <- MAX(arr[i], current + arr[i])
      best    <- MAX(best, current)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
py:
arr = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]

current = best = arr[0]

for i in range(1, len(arr)):
    current = max(arr[i], current + arr[i])
    best = max(best, current)

print(best)
trap: Starting both variables at 0. If every element is negative, the answer wrongly becomes 0. Start from arr[0] instead.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — the brute force over all subarrays is O(n²)

t: Maximum sum of a subarray of size k
layman: A window of 3 seats sliding down a row. When it moves, one person leaves and one enters — you adjust the total instead of recounting everyone.
task: Find the maximum sum of any k consecutive elements.
approach: Build the first window sum with a small loop over the first k elements.
From index k onward, slide: subtract arr[i - k] (leaving) and add arr[i] (entering).
Keep the champion max after every slide.
pseudo:
START
  windowSum <- SUM of first k elements
  best <- windowSum
  FOR i FROM k TO n - 1
      windowSum <- windowSum - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
      best <- MAX(best, windowSum)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
py:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]
k = 3

window = sum(arr[:k])
best = window

for i in range(k, len(arr)):
    window = window - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
    best = max(best, window)

print(best)
trap: Recomputing the whole window sum with an inner loop. That is O(n×k) — the entire point of the window is to avoid it.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — brute force is O(n×k)

t: Minimum sum of a subarray of size k
layman: Same sliding window, opposite champion. You are hunting the quietest three days instead of the busiest.
task: Find the minimum sum of any k consecutive elements.
approach: Identical structure to problem 76.
Only two things change: the comparison becomes min, and the starting champion is the first window.
Because the first window seeds the champion, no MAX_VALUE trick is needed here.
pseudo:
START
  windowSum <- SUM of first k elements
  best <- windowSum
  FOR i FROM k TO n - 1
      windowSum <- windowSum - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
      best <- MIN(best, windowSum)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
py:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 5, 50, 60, 2]
k = 3

window = sum(arr[:k])
best = window

for i in range(k, len(arr)):
    window = window - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
    best = min(best, window)

print(best)
trap: Seeding best with 0 instead of the first window sum. With all-positive numbers, 0 always wins and your answer is always 0.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Average of every window of size k
layman: A rolling 3-day average, like a moving temperature reading. The sum slides; you just divide at each stop.
task: Print the average of every group of k consecutive elements.
approach: Maintain the window sum exactly as before.
Divide by k for each window and store or print the result.
Use a decimal division — integer division would hide the fractional part.
pseudo:
START
  windowSum <- SUM of first k elements
  PRINT windowSum / k
  FOR i FROM k TO n - 1
      windowSum <- windowSum - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
      PRINT windowSum / k
  END FOR
END
py:
arr = [1, 3, 2, 6, -1, 4, 1, 8, 2]
k = 5

window = sum(arr[:k])
print(window / k, end=" ")

for i in range(k, len(arr)):
    window = window - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
    print(window / k, end=" ")
trap: Keeping the sum as an int and dividing by an int k. In Java, 11 / 5 gives 2, not 2.2.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: First negative number in every window of size k
layman: For each 3-day stretch, report the first loss-making day. You keep a short list of loss days currently inside the window.
task: For every window of size k, print the first negative number in it, or 0 if there is none.
approach: Keep a list of the INDEXES of negative numbers currently inside the window.
When the window slides, drop any index that has fallen off the left edge.
The front of the list is the answer for the current window; an empty list means 0.
pseudo:
START
  negatives <- EMPTY LIST
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      IF arr[i] < 0 THEN ADD i TO negatives
      IF i >= k - 1 THEN
          WHILE negatives NOT EMPTY AND front(negatives) <= i - k
              REMOVE front
          END WHILE
          IF negatives EMPTY THEN PRINT 0
          ELSE PRINT arr[front(negatives)]
      END IF
  END FOR
END
trap: Storing the negative VALUES instead of their indexes. Without an index you cannot tell when a value has slid out of the window.
cx: Time O(n) — each index enters and leaves once · Space O(k)

t: Maximum vowels in a substring of size k
layman: The window now counts how many vowels are inside it. Sliding costs one check on the letter leaving and one on the letter entering.
task: Find the maximum number of vowels in any substring of length k.
approach: Count vowels in the first k characters.
When sliding, subtract 1 if the outgoing character was a vowel, add 1 if the incoming one is.
Keep the champion count.
pseudo:
START
  count <- vowels in first k characters
  best <- count
  FOR i FROM k TO n - 1
      IF s[i] is vowel THEN count <- count + 1
      IF s[i - k] is vowel THEN count <- count - 1
      best <- MAX(best, count)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
trap: Adding the incoming character but forgetting to remove the outgoing one. The count only ever grows and the answer becomes meaningless.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Smallest subarray with sum at least target
layman: The window can now stretch and shrink. Grow it until the total is big enough, then squeeze from the left as long as it stays big enough.
task: Find the length of the shortest continuous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to the target.
approach: right expands the window and adds to the sum.
While the sum satisfies the condition, record the length and shrink from the left.
Shrinking is what finds the SMALLEST window — expanding alone would only find any window.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; sum <- 0 ; best <- INFINITY
  FOR right FROM 0 TO n - 1
      sum <- sum + arr[right]
      WHILE sum >= target
          best <- MIN(best, right - left + 1)
          sum  <- sum - arr[left]
          left <- left + 1
      END WHILE
  END FOR
  PRINT best (or 0 if never satisfied)
END
py:
arr = [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]
target = 7

left, total = 0, 0
best = float("inf")

for right in range(len(arr)):
    total += arr[right]

    while total >= target:
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        total -= arr[left]
        left += 1

print(0 if best == float("inf") else best)
trap: Using if instead of while for the shrink step. One shrink per expansion is not enough — you may need several to reach the smallest window.
cx: Time O(n) — each pointer moves forward at most n times · Space O(1)

t: Longest substring without repeating characters
layman: A window that must never contain the same letter twice. When a repeat enters, you slide the left edge past the previous copy.
task: Find the length of the longest substring with all distinct characters.
approach: Keep a map of character -> its most recent index.
When a repeat appears inside the current window, jump left to just after the previous occurrence.
Update the best length at every step: right - left + 1.
pseudo:
START
  last <- EMPTY MAP
  left <- 0 ; best <- 0
  FOR right FROM 0 TO n - 1
      c <- s[right]
      IF last HAS c AND last[c] >= left THEN
          left <- last[c] + 1
      END IF
      last[c] <- right
      best <- MAX(best, right - left + 1)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
trap: Moving left without the last[c] >= left check. An old occurrence that already fell outside the window would drag left backwards and break everything.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(k) for the distinct characters

t: Longest subarray with at most k distinct values
layman: A basket that can hold at most k types of fruit. Keep adding fruit; when a third type appears, drop fruit from the left until you are back to k types.
task: Find the length of the longest continuous subarray containing at most k distinct values.
approach: Keep a frequency map of what is currently inside the window.
Expand right and add the incoming value.
While the map has more than k keys, shrink from the left, decreasing counts and removing keys that hit zero.
pseudo:
START
  freq <- EMPTY MAP ; left <- 0 ; best <- 0
  FOR right FROM 0 TO n - 1
      freq[arr[right]] <- freq[arr[right]] + 1
      WHILE size(freq) > k
          freq[arr[left]] <- freq[arr[left]] - 1
          IF freq[arr[left]] = 0 THEN REMOVE arr[left] FROM freq
          left <- left + 1
      END WHILE
      best <- MAX(best, right - left + 1)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
trap: Decreasing the count but never deleting keys that reach zero. The map size then stays too high and the window never grows again.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(k)

t: Longest run of 1s after flipping at most k zeros
layman: You are allowed to repaint k black tiles white. Slide a window that never contains more than k black tiles, and measure the longest one.
task: Given an array of 0s and 1s, find the longest continuous stretch of 1s if you may flip at most k zeros.
approach: Track how many zeros the window currently contains.
Expand right; if the incoming value is 0, increase the zero counter.
While the zero count exceeds k, shrink from the left, decreasing the counter when a 0 leaves.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; zeros <- 0 ; best <- 0
  FOR right FROM 0 TO n - 1
      IF arr[right] = 0 THEN zeros <- zeros + 1
      WHILE zeros > k
          IF arr[left] = 0 THEN zeros <- zeros - 1
          left <- left + 1
      END WHILE
      best <- MAX(best, right - left + 1)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
trap: Shrinking the window by one blindly on every violation. The while loop must keep shrinking until the zero count is legal again.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Longest subarray with sum at most k
layman: A shopping trolley with a spending limit. Keep adding items; when you cross the budget, remove items from the front until you are back under it.
task: Find the length of the longest continuous subarray whose sum does not exceed k. All values are positive.
approach: Expand right and add to the sum.
While the sum exceeds k, shrink from the left.
After the window is legal again, record its length. This only works because all values are positive.
pseudo:
START
  left <- 0 ; sum <- 0 ; best <- 0
  FOR right FROM 0 TO n - 1
      sum <- sum + arr[right]
      WHILE sum > k
          sum  <- sum - arr[left]
          left <- left + 1
      END WHILE
      best <- MAX(best, right - left + 1)
  END FOR
  PRINT best
END
py:
arr = [3, 1, 2, 7, 4, 2, 1, 1, 5]
k = 8

left, total, best = 0, 0, 0

for right in range(len(arr)):
    total += arr[right]

    while total > k:
        total -= arr[left]
        left += 1

    best = max(best, right - left + 1)

print(best)
trap: Using this pattern with negative numbers present. Shrinking may then INCREASE the sum, so the window logic no longer holds — use prefix sums with a map instead.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Count windows of size k with sum above a threshold
layman: How many 3-day stretches crossed the sales target? Slide the window, and tally each stretch that qualifies.
task: Count how many subarrays of size k have a sum strictly greater than the given threshold.
approach: Standard fixed window sum.
After each slide, compare with the threshold and increment the counter if it qualifies.
Do not forget to test the very first window before the sliding loop starts.
pseudo:
START
  windowSum <- SUM of first k elements
  count <- 0
  IF windowSum > threshold THEN count <- count + 1
  FOR i FROM k TO n - 1
      windowSum <- windowSum - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
      IF windowSum > threshold THEN count <- count + 1
  END FOR
  PRINT count
END
py:
arr = [2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5, 8]
k, threshold = 3, 12

window = sum(arr[:k])
count = 1 if window > threshold else 0

for i in range(k, len(arr)):
    window = window - arr[i - k] + arr[i]
    if window > threshold:
        count += 1

print(count)
trap: Testing only inside the sliding loop. The first window never gets checked, so a qualifying opening stretch is silently missed.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1)

t: Maximum of every window of size k
layman: Report the tallest person inside the window at every position. The honest solution rechecks k people each time; the clever one keeps a shortlist.
task: Print the maximum element of every window of size k. Write the straightforward version first, then the optimised one.
approach: Simple version: for each window start, loop through its k elements and take the max — O(n×k).
Optimised: keep a deque of indexes whose values are in decreasing order.
Before adding a new index, remove all smaller values from the back — they can never be the max again. The front is always the answer.
pseudo:
// Optimised
  dq <- EMPTY DEQUE of indexes
  FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
      REMOVE front IF front <= i - k
      WHILE dq NOT EMPTY AND arr[back] <= arr[i]
          REMOVE back
      END WHILE
      ADD i TO back
      IF i >= k - 1 THEN PRINT arr[front]
  END FOR
trap: Storing values in the deque instead of indexes. You then cannot tell when the front element has slid out of the window.
cx: Brute force O(n×k) · Deque version O(n) · Space O(k)

t: Binary search on a sorted array
layman: Finding a word in a dictionary. You open the middle page, decide which half the word is in, and throw the other half away. Every step halves the work.
task: Find the index of a target value in a sorted array, or -1 if it is absent.
approach: low starts at 0, high at n - 1.
Compute mid, compare arr[mid] with the target.
Target smaller means search the left half (high = mid - 1); larger means the right half (low = mid + 1).
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; high <- n - 1
  WHILE low <= high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF arr[mid] = target THEN RETURN mid
      ELSE IF arr[mid] < target THEN low <- mid + 1
      ELSE high <- mid - 1
  END WHILE
  RETURN -1
END
trap: Using low < high instead of <=. When the range narrows to one element, that element never gets checked.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1) · Requires a SORTED array

t: First occurrence of a repeated value
layman: You found the value, but there may be copies to your left. So you note this position and keep searching leftward instead of stopping.
task: In a sorted array with duplicates, find the index of the FIRST occurrence of the target.
approach: Run a normal binary search.
On a match, record the index but do NOT return — move high to mid - 1 to hunt further left.
When the loop ends, the last recorded index is the earliest match.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; high <- n - 1 ; answer <- -1
  WHILE low <= high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF arr[mid] = target THEN
          answer <- mid
          high <- mid - 1        // keep looking left
      ELSE IF arr[mid] < target THEN low <- mid + 1
      ELSE high <- mid - 1
  END WHILE
  RETURN answer
END
trap: Returning immediately on the first match. Binary search may land in the middle of the duplicate block, so you get index 2 instead of 1.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1)

t: Last occurrence of a repeated value
layman: Same idea, mirrored. Note the position and keep searching rightward for a later copy.
task: In a sorted array with duplicates, find the index of the LAST occurrence of the target.
approach: Same structure as problem 89.
On a match, record the index and set low = mid + 1 to search right.
The final recorded index is the latest match.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; high <- n - 1 ; answer <- -1
  WHILE low <= high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF arr[mid] = target THEN
          answer <- mid
          low <- mid + 1        // keep looking right
      ELSE IF arr[mid] < target THEN low <- mid + 1
      ELSE high <- mid - 1
  END WHILE
  RETURN answer
END
trap: Copying the first-occurrence code and changing only the comment. The direction line must change from high = mid - 1 to low = mid + 1.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1)

t: Count occurrences in a sorted array
layman: If you know where the block of copies begins and where it ends, the count is just a subtraction — no counting one by one.
task: Count how many times the target appears in a sorted array, faster than O(n).
approach: Find the first occurrence with one binary search.
Find the last occurrence with another.
Count = last - first + 1. If first is -1, the count is 0.
pseudo:
START
  first <- firstOccurrence(arr, target)
  IF first = -1 THEN RETURN 0
  last  <- lastOccurrence(arr, target)
  RETURN last - first + 1
END
trap: Forgetting the +1. Indices 1 to 3 hold three elements, not two — always test with a block of exactly one element.
cx: Time O(log n) — two binary searches · Space O(1). Counting by scanning would be O(n)

t: Insert position in a sorted array
layman: A new student joins a line arranged by height. Where should they stand? If they already exist, return that spot; otherwise return where they would slot in.
task: Return the index of the target, or the index where it should be inserted to keep the array sorted.
approach: Run a standard binary search.
If the target is found, return mid.
If the loop ends without a match, low is exactly the insert position — that is the useful property of this loop.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; high <- n - 1
  WHILE low <= high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF arr[mid] = target THEN RETURN mid
      ELSE IF arr[mid] < target THEN low <- mid + 1
      ELSE high <- mid - 1
  END WHILE
  RETURN low
END
trap: Returning -1 when the target is absent. This problem wants the position, and low already holds it when the loop exits.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1)

t: Integer square root using binary search
layman: Guessing a number between 1 and n. Guess the middle, square it, and see whether you guessed too high or too low. Binary search does not need an array.
task: Find the integer square root of n — the largest whole number whose square is at most n.
approach: The answer lives somewhere between 1 and n, so search that RANGE rather than an array.
If mid × mid is at most n, mid is a candidate — record it and try bigger.
Otherwise mid is too large; search lower. Use long for the square to avoid overflow.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 1 ; high <- n ; answer <- 0
  WHILE low <= high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF mid * mid <= n THEN
          answer <- mid
          low <- mid + 1
      ELSE
          high <- mid - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
  PRINT answer
END
trap: Computing mid * mid as int for large n. It overflows and turns negative, which passes the check and gives a nonsense answer.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1) — trying every number would be O(√n) or worse

t: Search in a rotated sorted array
layman: A sorted list that someone cut and swapped: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. At every step, one half is still properly sorted — find that half and decide from it.
task: Find the index of a target in a sorted array that has been rotated at an unknown point.
approach: Compute mid as usual. Then ask which side is sorted: if arr[low] <= arr[mid], the left half is sorted.
If the target lies inside that sorted half range, search there. Otherwise search the other half.
The same halving still applies, so the cost stays logarithmic.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; high <- n - 1
  WHILE low <= high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF arr[mid] = target THEN RETURN mid
      IF arr[low] <= arr[mid] THEN            // left half sorted
          IF target >= arr[low] AND target < arr[mid] THEN high <- mid - 1
          ELSE low <- mid + 1
      ELSE                                     // right half sorted
          IF target > arr[mid] AND target <= arr[high] THEN low <- mid + 1
          ELSE high <- mid - 1
      END IF
  END WHILE
  RETURN -1
END
trap: Applying plain binary search. The array is not globally sorted, so comparing the target with arr[mid] alone sends you into the wrong half.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1)

t: Find a peak element
layman: Walking a mountain range in fog. If the ground rises to your right, a peak must exist somewhere over there — so throw the left side away.
task: Find any element that is greater than both of its neighbours. Edges count as having a boundary of negative infinity.
approach: Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1].
If arr[mid] < arr[mid+1], the slope rises to the right — a peak lies to the right, so low = mid + 1.
Otherwise the peak is at mid or to its left, so high = mid. The loop uses low < high and ends on the answer.
pseudo:
START
  low <- 0 ; high <- n - 1
  WHILE low < high
      mid <- low + (high - low) / 2
      IF arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1] THEN
          low <- mid + 1
      ELSE
          high <- mid
      END IF
  END WHILE
  RETURN low
END
trap: Using low <= high here. With high = mid the range never shrinks in that branch and you loop forever.
cx: Time O(log n) · Space O(1) — and it works without the array being fully sorted

t: Find the middle element with fast and slow pointers
layman: Two people on a track. Slow takes one step, fast takes two. When fast reaches the end, slow is standing exactly at the middle.
task: Find the middle element of an array without using its length.
approach: slow starts at 0, fast starts at 0.
Each round: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2.
When fast can no longer move, slow is at the midpoint. Because fast covers twice the distance, slow covers exactly half.
pseudo:
START
  slow <- 0 ; fast <- 0
  WHILE fast < n - 1
      slow <- slow + 1
      fast <- fast + 2
  END WHILE
  PRINT arr[slow]
END
py:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

slow = fast = 0

while fast < len(arr) - 1:
    slow += 1
    fast += 2

print(arr[slow])
trap: Checking only fast < n. With an even count, fast can step past the end — the guard must leave room for the double step.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — the real payoff comes with linked lists, where length is unknown

t: Detect a cycle in a linked list
layman: Two runners on a track. If the track is a closed loop, the faster runner will eventually lap the slower one and they will meet. On a straight road, they never do.
task: Check whether a linked list contains a cycle.
io: List: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> back to 2 Output: true (cycle detected) List: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null Output: false
approach: slow moves one node at a time, fast moves two.
If fast or fast.next becomes null, the list ended — no cycle.
If slow and fast ever point to the same node, they are going round a loop.
pseudo:
START
  slow <- head ; fast <- head
  WHILE fast != NULL AND fast.next != NULL
      slow <- slow.next
      fast <- fast.next.next
      IF slow = fast THEN RETURN TRUE
  END WHILE
  RETURN FALSE
END
trap: Checking only fast != null. You then call fast.next.next when fast.next is null and get a NullPointerException.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — a HashSet solution also works but needs O(n) memory

t: Happy number
layman: Keep replacing a number by the sum of the squares of its digits. Either you reach 1, or you fall into a loop forever — the same cycle detection, without a linked list.
task: A number is happy if repeatedly summing the squares of its digits eventually reaches 1. Determine whether a number is happy.
approach: Write a helper that returns the sum of the squares of the digits.
slow applies the helper once per round, fast applies it twice.
If fast reaches 1, the number is happy. If slow and fast meet at anything else, you are in a loop.
pseudo:
FUNCTION next(n)
  sum <- 0
  WHILE n > 0
      d <- n MOD 10
      sum <- sum + d * d
      n <- n / 10
  END WHILE
  RETURN sum
END FUNCTION

START
  slow <- n ; fast <- next(n)
  WHILE fast != 1 AND slow != fast
      slow <- next(slow)
      fast <- next(next(fast))
  END WHILE
  RETURN fast = 1
END
py:
def next_num(n):
    total = 0
    while n > 0:
        d = n % 10
        total += d * d
        n = n // 10
    return total

def is_happy(n):
    slow = n
    fast = next_num(n)

    while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
        slow = next_num(slow)
        fast = next_num(next_num(fast))

    return fast == 1

print(is_happy(19))
print(is_happy(2))
trap: Looping without any cycle guard. An unhappy number cycles forever and your program hangs — that is exactly what the fast pointer prevents.
cx: Time O(log n) per step, effectively constant rounds · Space O(1)

t: Find the duplicate number without modifying the array
layman: Treat each value as an arrow pointing to another index. A repeated value means two arrows land on the same place — which creates a loop you can detect.
task: An array of n+1 numbers holds values from 1 to n. Exactly one value repeats. Find it without sorting and without extra memory.
approach: Phase 1: move slow one hop (slow = arr[slow]) and fast two hops until they meet inside the loop.
Phase 2: reset slow to the start, then move BOTH one hop at a time.
Where they meet again is the entry point of the loop — which is the duplicated value.
pseudo:
START
  slow <- arr[0] ; fast <- arr[arr[0]]
  WHILE slow != fast
      slow <- arr[slow]
      fast <- arr[arr[fast]]
  END WHILE

  slow <- 0
  WHILE slow != fast
      slow <- arr[slow]
      fast <- arr[fast]
  END WHILE
  RETURN slow
END
py:
def find_duplicate(arr):
    slow = arr[0]
    fast = arr[arr[0]]

    while slow != fast:
        slow = arr[slow]
        fast = arr[arr[fast]]

    slow = 0
    while slow != fast:
        slow = arr[slow]
        fast = arr[fast]

    return slow

print(find_duplicate([1, 3, 4, 2, 2]))
trap: Stopping after phase 1. The first meeting point is somewhere inside the loop, not necessarily the duplicate — phase 2 is what pinpoints the entry.
cx: Time O(n) · Space O(1) — sorting would be O(n log n), a HashSet O(n) memory

t: Nth node from the end in one pass
layman: Give the first pointer an n-step head start. Then move both together. When the leader reaches the end, the follower is exactly n places behind it.
task: Find the nth node from the end of a linked list, without counting the length first.
approach: Move the fast pointer n steps ahead first.
Then move fast and slow together, one step each.
When fast falls off the end, slow is sitting on the answer — the gap between them never changes.
pseudo:
START
  slow <- head ; fast <- head
  REPEAT n TIMES
      fast <- fast.next
  END REPEAT

  WHILE fast != NULL
      slow <- slow.next
      fast <- fast.next
  END WHILE
  RETURN slow
END
trap: Skipping the null check during the head start. If n is larger than the list length, fast.next crashes before the main loop even begins.
cx: Time O(n) single pass · Space O(1) — counting the length first would need two passes
